summary: Amends RFC 4462 by defining a new GSS-API key exchange method that uses SHA-2 for integrity and deprecates weak Diffie-Hellman groups. The goal is to modernize the cryptographic primitives used by GSS key exchanges in SSH.

eli5.summary: An old lock used weak parts. This swaps in stronger parts, so the secret handshake that starts a secure connection is harder to break.

questions: what is gss-api key exchange in ssh
which ssh gss kex methods use sha-256
subtitle: New SHA-2 and elliptic-curve key exchange methods for SSH sessions that authenticate through GSS-API, replacing SHA-1 ones.

tldr.problem: The SSH key exchange methods that use GSS-API (defined in RFC 4462) rely on SHA-1 and on Diffie-Hellman groups that are now considered too weak.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8732 registers new method families that pair SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 with larger MODP groups (group14 to group18) or with elliptic curves (NIST P-256, P-384, P-521, X25519, X448), and marks the old SHA-1 methods SHOULD NOT.
tldr.outcome: Implementations get modern, GSS-API-authenticated key exchange options; the message flow is the same as before, only the primitives change.

today: RFC 8732 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2020. It updates RFC 4462, and the metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Secure Shell (SSH) GSS-API methods in RFC 4462 let SSH use the Generic Security Service API (GSS-API, RFC 2743) for authentication and key exchange. RFC 4462 defines three exchange methods, all based on Diffie-Hellman (DH) groups and SHA-1.

RFC 8732 updates RFC 4462 with new methods for environments that want to use the SHA-2 family of hash functions.
sections.eli5: SSH can borrow a login system from somewhere else to prove who you are. This document gives that borrowed system stronger tools for building a secret key.

sections.title: Why the Old Methods Needed Replacing
sections.content:
The RFC gives two reasons. SHA-1 has known security concerns (it cites RFC 6194), and modular exponentiation (MODP) groups with fewer than 2048 bits are also a concern. So it proposes SHA-2 hashes (RFC 6234) with DH group14, group15, group16, group17 and group18 (RFC 3526).

It also adds Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) with the NIST P-256, P-384 and P-521 curves, plus the X25519 and X448 curves.

For the DH groups, only SHA-256 and SHA-512 are used, following RFC 8268. For the NIST curves, the same curve-to-hash pairing as RFC 5656 is used, for consistency.
sections.eli5: The old locks were still working but experts worried that someone clever could pick them. So the document offers sturdier locks.

sections.title: Finite-Field Diffie-Hellman Methods
sections.content:
Each new method is a family of names that covers any GSS-API mechanism for one group and hash combination. The method name is the family prefix followed by the base64 encoding of the MD5 hash of the ASN.1 DER encoding of the GSS-API mechanism's OID. The IESG is the change controller of these names, which does not mean the IESG controls the GSS-API mechanism itself.

The methods run the GSS-API-authenticated DH exchange from Section 2.1 of RFC 4462. Two families are marked SHOULD/RECOMMENDED: gss-group14-sha256-* and gss-group16-sha512-*. The other three (group15, group17, group18) are MAY/OPTIONAL.

The MD5 hash is only used to turn a mechanism OID into a fixed-length part of the method name. It is not the hash that protects the key exchange.
sections.eli5: Each method has a name tag made of a recipe (group plus hash) and a code for the login system in use. That way both sides can agree on exactly which recipe to follow.

sections.title: The Elliptic Curve Key Exchange
sections.content:
The ECDH methods combine the scheme of RFC 4462 Section 2.1 with Section 4 of RFC 5656. The client starts the GSS context with GSS_Init_sec_context() and the server answers with GSS_Accept_sec_context(). The client sends its ephemeral public key Q_C in the first message. If the server gets more than one key or none, the exchange MUST fail.

The client MUST set mutual_req_flag and integ_req_flag to true, and deleg_req_flag MAY be set to ask for delegation. When the context is complete, both sides check that mutual_state and integ_avail are true, or the exchange MUST fail. For NIST curves, compressed point representation MUST cause failure. For X25519 and X448, implementations MUST abort if the shared secret is all zero.

Both sides compute the shared secret K and the exchange hash H over the version strings, both SSH_MSG_KEXINIT payloads, the host key K_S, both ephemeral public keys and K. The server runs GSS_GetMIC() on H, and the client checks it with GSS_VerifyMIC(). The host key message is OPTIONAL, and MUST NOT be sent when the null host key algorithm is used; an empty string then stands in for K_S.

Recommended ECDH families: gss-nistp256-sha256-* and gss-curve25519-sha256-* (SHOULD/RECOMMENDED); gss-nistp384-sha384-*, gss-nistp521-sha512-* and gss-curve448-sha512-* are MAY/OPTIONAL.
sections.eli5: Two people each make a secret number, swap a scrambled version, and end up with the same shared secret. A trusted third party stamps the result so each knows the other is real.

sections.title: Deprecated Algorithms
sections.content:
Because of their small key lengths, and because they are no longer strong against brute-force attacks, three existing method families are now SHOULD NOT: gss-group1-sha1-*, gss-group14-sha1-* and gss-gex-sha1-*.

The document does not remove them. It tells implementations not to use them.
sections.eli5: The old, weak methods get a sign saying please do not use. They are not banned, just discouraged.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
For the finite-field methods, only a different hash and larger groups are used, so all original security considerations of RFC 4462 still apply. For the elliptic curve methods, the exchange closely follows RFC 5656, so its considerations also apply.

Delegation deserves care. If a GSS-API mechanism delegates credentials when deleg_req_flag is set, the client must be sure the acceptor is the intended target. Some mechanism implementations, such as commonly used krb5 libraries, may use insecure DNS resolution to canonicalize the target name. A spoofed DNS response that points to an attacker's machine could then lead the user to silently delegate credentials, letting the attacker impersonate the user.
sections.eli5: Be careful who you hand your keys to. If someone tricks the phone book, you might give your key to a stranger.

sections.title: IANA Registry Changes
sections.content: IANA lists RFC 8732 as the reference for the three deprecated SHA-1 entries in the SSH Protocol Parameters key exchange method names registry. It also added the ten new families: five DH (group14-sha256, group15-sha512, group16-sha512, group17-sha512, group18-sha512) and five ECDH (nistp256-sha256, nistp384-sha384, nistp521-sha512, curve25519-sha256, curve448-sha512), each with the gss- prefix and a trailing wildcard.
sections.eli5: The official list of method names got ten new entries, so everyone spells them the same way.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_INIT
messages.note: GSS output token plus the client's ephemeral public key Q_C.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_HOSTKEY
messages.note: Optional; carries the server host key K_S.

messages.label: SSH_MSG_KEXGSS_COMPLETE
messages.note: Server's ephemeral key Q_S and the MIC of H.
